title: Claim an item with a secret link

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL. Audited commit db295c1, working tree clean, sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict. Ten of eleven requirements are met, most of them well. Req 1 is not, and Req 1 is the requirement this sprint exists to get right.

BLOCKING ISSUE - Req 1 - app/claim/[token]/route.ts line 75 and line 82
The claim token is interpolated into the form action of the claim page, so it appears verbatim in the body of a GET response: <form method="POST" action="/claim/TOKEN">. Req 1 states that POST /api/items is the only path in the system that ever emits the token, and that it must never appear in any GET response. This is a second path. The QA1 criterion for Req 1 is more specific still: confirm the claim page own rendering still excludes it, and it pre-empts the obvious defence in its own words - a claim page that ships the token is a leak even though the viewer already has it in their URL, because it widens the hole beyond one path. That clause was written to foreclose exactly the argument this code invites, so I am not going to accept it.
Demonstrated, not argued. I compiled the shipped route file and ran its own emitted escapeHtml and renderItemHtml against a known token - no reimplementation, the files own bytes. The 200 body for an unclaimed item contains the token exactly once, in the form action. For a claimed item the count is zero, because the form is not rendered, which confirms the form action is the sole carrier and therefore the whole of the fix.
Being straight about severity: this discloses nothing to a party who does not already hold the token, since only a holder can request that URL, and Req 9 headers cover the index and referer paths. This is a conformance failure against an invariant this sprint deliberately defined as one path wide, not an exploitable disclosure. I am calling it because the requirement and its criterion are unambiguous, because the sprints own stated central risk is the exception growing beyond one path, and because the fix is one attribute.
REQUIRED FIX: drop the action attribute (or set it empty) and delete the claimAction const. A form with no action submits to the current document URL by definition, which is already /claim/TOKEN, so the POST handler still receives the same params.token and nothing else changes. Re-audit will be quick - one file, one line.

ON THE QUESTION DEV TEAM ASKED - Route Handler versus Page for the claim surface: the decision is correct and the reasoning is sound. A Page under a dynamic segment carries the requested segment value in its RSC payload regardless of what the component renders, so byte-identical not-found bodies are impossible to guarantee from inside the page. A Route Handler returns exactly the bytes it constructs, which turns Req 5 from a discipline property into a structural one - the same instinct as making token containment structural through the type system rather than through every caller remembering to strip a field. Finding it by diffing real output rather than reading the requirement is the right way to have found it, and flagging it to me explicitly was right too. The irony is worth stating plainly: having taken control of every byte on the page precisely so nothing could leak into it, the implementation then interpolated the secret into one of those bytes by hand.

REQUIREMENTS COVERAGE:
Req 1: NOT MET - see above. Everything else about containment is right: ITEM_COLUMNS excludes claim_token, listItems, findItemByClaimToken and claimItemByToken all return plain Item, CreatedItem is returned by exactly one function and read in exactly one place, no SELECT * anywhere, and every console call takes the caught error and never an item object. The board destructures claimToken off before the item reaches list state. The defect is one line, not a pattern.
Req 2: MET. Link shown once in a readOnly input that selects on focus, with an explicit warning that it will not be shown again, plus a copy button whose failure path degrades to manual selection rather than to nothing.
Req 3: MET. Lookup is by token only. There is no id-plus-token path to distinguish a real id from a wrong token.
Req 4: MET. Item plus one button. No edit, no delete, no unclaim.
Req 5: MET, and met structurally. NOT_FOUND_HTML is one frozen literal with no per-request interpolation of any kind, returned from one function, with one status and one header object. Unknown, malformed, and no-longer-matching tokens all reach it through the same single branch, so there are no sibling branches that could drift apart.
Req 6: MET. The write lives only in POST. GET reads and never mutates. The form is a real method=POST form, so a prefetch, crawler or link preview cannot fire it. The update is an unconditional SET claimed = TRUE keyed on the token, not a read-then-write, so replaying it is idempotent at the database level and cannot clobber a concurrent write. The token is verified on the write itself, not merely on the render that produced the button.
Req 7: MET. Grepped for any assignment of claimed to false and for any unclaim path: the only hit is the comment saying there is not one.
Req 8: MET. Strikethrough plus a literal (Claimed) text label, so it survives a colorblind viewer and a black-and-white screenshot. The item stays on the board and the email stays visible.
Req 9: MET as a static fact. Both X-Robots-Tag noindex and Referrer-Policy no-referrer are configured for /claim/:token. Arriving on the wire is LiveQA.
Req 10: MET, and this is the part I checked hardest because Req 5 and Req 10 pull against each other. The lookup wraps the query and returns an error sentinel distinct from null. In GET the error branch is tested and returned before the not-found branch can run. In POST the catch returns the error response and the not-found check is only reached when the query itself succeeded. A thrown database error has no path into the generic not-found response, so a poster holding a valid link under a dead database gets an error state and not a false this-does-not-exist. Both responses are generic, with no connection string, host, credential or driver detail; full detail goes to console.error only.
Req 11: MET. force-dynamic on the board and on the claim route, and the claim POST redirects 303 back to a fresh GET rather than rendering from the mutation response.

ALSO VERIFIED: npm run lint exit 0 and npm run build exit 0, both run by me; build lists /claim/[token] as dynamic, not static. The hand-built HTML is the new XSS surface in this sprint and it holds - I ran the real render function against a title of script-alert and an email crafted to break out of the href attribute. Both come back entity-escaped, no executable script, no attribute break-out. escapeHtml covers ampersand, angle brackets and both quote characters, and escapes the ampersand first, which is the ordering that avoids double-escaping.

NON-BLOCKING, not holding this gate:
1. lib/format.ts comment claims it is shared with components/claim-form.tsx, which does not exist - the claim surface was rebuilt as a route handler and the comment did not follow. Stale as written.
2. The POST redirect builds an absolute Location from request.url. Behind a proxy that can differ from the public origin; a relative Location would be immune. LiveQA exercises this path, so it will surface there if it is wrong.
3. app/layout.tsx still carries the default Create Next App metadata title, carried since sprint 1.

Fix the one line, commit, and send it back. LiveQA still owns the cold-client token hunt, the byte-identical comparison across three bad tokens, the GET-does-not-claim check, the headers on the wire, and above all forcing a real database failure against the claim page. Dev Team has already stood the poisoned preview up, which should spare that criterion a fourth round of friction.
